opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something we thought about a lot in our "impossible languages" work. One caveat up front: GPT-2, like most modern language models, wasn't designed to be a model of human cognition. It was designed to predict the next token well. So when people make claims about what these models can or can't tell us about human language learning, I think we have to be careful about what the architecture actually encodes.

There are a few places where I think changes could make it more plausible as a cognitive model. The first is the data regime. Humans learn language from maybe tens of millions of words in childhood, while these models see billions or trillions of tokens. Training on developmentally realistic amounts of data, like in the BabyLM challenge, is one step toward a fairer comparison.

The second is the inductive biases in the architecture itself. A standard transformer has full access to the entire context window at every step, with no real memory constraints. Humans process language incrementally and have limited working memory. So you could imagine adding things like recency biases, locality constraints, or memory bottlenecks, and then asking whether those biases make the model more like humans, for example by making it find certain unnatural, "impossible" language patterns harder to learn.

That connects to what we found. Even without these changes, GPT-2 did struggle more with some impossible languages than with natural English, which pushes back on the strong claim that these models can learn anything equally well. But the differences weren't always as clean as you might want. Some of the patterns that are impossible for humans, like rules based on counting word positions, were still learnable to some degree. Positional encodings are a good example: they give the model a very direct way to count positions, which humans don't seem to rely on for grammar. So modifying or removing those encodings is an interesting experiment.

Finally there's tokenization. Subword tokenizers like BPE are engineering choices, not something that reflects how children segment speech. Moving toward character-level or byte-level modeling, or architectures that learn their own segmentation, could make these models better testbeds.

So overall, I see these models less as finished models of the mind and more as a flexible experimental tool. By systematically changing the architecture and the training conditions, we can start asking which biases are actually necessary to get human-like learning behavior. I think that's where a lot of the exciting work is going to be.

r001.rationale: The response proposes adding human-like biases such as recency, locality, or memory limits and evaluating whether they make impossible language patterns harder to learn, as a way to make the model more cognitively plausible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the motivation for a lot of this work comes from a very simple observation about how language models and humans actually differ, and a lot of that difference starts at the input. When you train a model like GPT-2, the first thing you do is run text through a tokenizer, usually something like byte-pair encoding, which chunks the text into subword units based on frequency statistics. And those units are not linguistic units in any principled sense. They don't correspond to morphemes, they don't correspond to syllables, and they certainly don't correspond to anything a child is exposed to when acquiring language. A child hears a continuous stream of speech, or sees a continuous stream of characters when learning to read, and has to figure out where the meaningful boundaries are. The tokenizer hands the model those boundaries for free, and sometimes hands it boundaries that are just wrong.

So one direction we've explored is what happens if you get rid of that assumption and let the model operate over bytes or characters directly. The problem, of course, is that this makes your sequences much longer, which is expensive for a transformer. The way we've approached that is to introduce a mechanism that lets the model learn to pool or chunk the input itself, dynamically, as part of the same objective it's already optimizing. So rather than a fixed vocabulary imposed from outside, the model develops its own sense of what the units are. And what's interesting from a cognitive standpoint is that the segmentations it arrives at tend to align much better with things like morphological boundaries than BPE does, even though we never told it anything about morphology. That's a nice result because there's a long literature in psycholinguistics suggesting that humans are doing something similar, using statistical regularities to discover units at multiple levels.

The other change I'd highlight has to do with how the model processes information over time. Standard GPT-2 attends over the full context with no real constraint on memory or recency, and that's obviously not how people work. Humans have a limited working memory and show strong locality effects, where things that are nearby are easier to integrate than things that are far away. There's been work, both from us and from others, on building in those kinds of inductive biases, for instance by modifying the attention mechanism to have a recency preference or a bounded memory. And what you find is that these constrained models often do a better job of predicting human reading behavior, things like eye-tracking measures or reading times, even when their raw perplexity is slightly worse. Which I think is a really important point. If what you care about is cognitive plausibility, then the best language model in the engineering sense isn't necessarily the best model of the human.

So the broader way I'd frame it is that GPT-2 is a really convenient starting point because it's small enough to train from scratch, it's well understood, and it already captures a lot of syntax. But out of the box it bakes in a bunch of assumptions, about tokenization, about memory, about how much data it needs, that don't match what we know about people. Each architectural change is a way of relaxing one of those assumptions and asking whether the model's behavior moves closer to or further from what humans do. When it moves closer, that tells you something about which ingredients matter, and that's really what I find exciting about this line of research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learned segmentation, memory constraints, and human-like processing, but does not propose architectures that favor natural languages over impossible languages.

astra-6.text:
I think GPT-2 gives us a useful starting point because it learns to predict language from context. But being good at predicting the next word doesn’t necessarily mean it learns or processes language the way humans do.

One way to explore that is to change the architecture’s inductive biases—the kinds of patterns it’s naturally inclined to learn. Could we build in constraints on memory or attention, for example, and see whether that produces behavior that looks more like human language processing? Or could we introduce a stronger bias toward hierarchical structure and see how that affects generalization?

The important thing would be to test those changes against human behavior, rather than assume that a particular architectural feature makes the model cognitively plausible. Does it learn from less data? Does it make similar errors? Does it struggle with the same kinds of sentences? That’s where architectural changes can become useful scientific experiments, beyond just improving performance on a language modeling benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architectural biases and testing for human-like processing, but it does not propose favoring natural languages over impossible languages.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by cognitively plausible. A model can predict language very well without necessarily processing it the way people do. So, with GPT-2, we can ask which aspects of its architecture are doing useful work and which reflect assumptions that don’t line up particularly well with human language processing.

One example is access to context. GPT-2 can attend directly to words throughout its context window, whereas people have memory limitations, and retrieving something we heard earlier isn’t always easy or reliable. Changing that mechanism could let us explore whether a model with more human-like memory constraints also shows patterns we see in human language behavior.

But I wouldn’t assume that a particular architectural change makes the model cognitively plausible on its own. The important step is testing it: does it make better predictions about where people struggle, what they learn, or how they generalize? That’s where these models can become useful tools for investigating language, beyond just generating it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human-like memory limits and testing language behavior, but it does not propose architectures that favor natural languages over impossible languages.
